title: Bipartite animal conflicts
label: idb
statement:
Given a hashmap where:

• Each key represents an animal.
• The value is a list of animals that cannot be placed on the same side as the key animal.

Determine whether all animals can be divided into two groups such that no conflicting animals are in the same group.

Example:
{1: [2], 3: [1, 2]} → Not valid
{1: [2], 2: [1, 3]} → Valid
provenance: Supplied by you from InterviewDB — the statement above is **verbatim**. Corroboration: InterviewDB only; the pattern is attested by 323 and 261.
clarify: An animal listed only as a value must still be placed.
A duplicate conflict (the same pair twice) is harmless.
An animal conflicting with itself is unsatisfiable.

stages.say: Given a map from each animal to the animals it cannot share a side with, can all animals be divided into two groups with no conflict inside a group?

stages.require: Add `(List<int> Left, List<int> Right) AnimalGrouping.Split(conflicts)`. Put the smallest animal id on the Left; return each list sorted.

flaw.ctx: You asked the assistant to check whether the animals can be split into two groups.
flaw.answer: Two defects. It colours **only the component containing the first key**, so a bad second component is never visited. And it walks the map as given — one-directional — so `{1:[2,3], 2:[3]}` is never seen as the triangle it is. The test "bad second component caught" fails.
flaw.fix: Build a symmetric adjacency list first, then start a BFS from every uncoloured node.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given a hashmap where:
> 
> • Each key represents an animal.
> • The value is a list of animals that cannot be placed on the same side as the key animal.
> 
> Determine whether all animals can be divided into two groups such that no conflicting animals are in the same group.
> 
> Example:
> {1: [2], 3: [1, 2]} → Not valid
> {1: [2], 2: [1, 3]} → Valid

You are seating animals on two sides, and some pairs must not share a side. The question is whether any such seating exists at all — not which one, and not how many.

A single boolean: does a valid two-way split exist. A natural follow-up asks for the two groups, which costs nothing extra.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
The input is a map, and a map is a bad way to express a symmetric relation. The first example declares `3: [1, 2]` but does **not** declare `1: [3]`. So either conflicts are mutual and the input is allowed to state each one once, or they are directional and mean something else.

Both examples are consistent with **mutual**, and "cannot be placed on the same side as" is symmetric in plain English, so mutual is the reading to take. Say that you are taking it. If conflicts were genuinely one-way the problem would be different and considerably stranger.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Conflicts are mutual. | If they were directional, "cannot be on the same side" would have to mean something asymmetric, and the problem is no longer bipartiteness. This is the assumption to state out loud. |
| An animal listed only as a value must still be placed. | If it can be ignored, the answer can change from invalid to valid. Building the adjacency symmetrically handles it automatically — which is a good reason to build it that way rather than colour the input map directly. |
| A duplicate conflict (the same pair twice) is harmless. | It produces a parallel edge. Colouring is unaffected. Worth one sentence, not more. |
| An animal conflicting with itself is unsatisfiable. | It cannot avoid its own side. Returning false is the only sensible answer; silently ignoring it would return a "valid" split that violates the constraint. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
The words "divided into two groups such that no conflicting pair shares a group" are the definition of a **bipartite graph**, and recognising that is the whole question. Everything after it is a standard walk.

The reason it is worth saying rather than just doing: once it is a graph question, the failure condition becomes something you can state precisely. A two-way split exists if and only if the graph contains **no odd cycle**. Walk the graph assigning alternating sides; if you ever reach a node that already has the same side as the one you came from, you have closed a cycle of odd length, and no assignment can work — not this one, not any.

That "not any" is the part a case-by-case attempt cannot give you. Trying to place animals greedily and backtracking would also find the answer, and would leave you unable to say why. The colouring argument tells you the answer is a property of the graph rather than of your search order.

The two places this goes wrong have nothing to do with the algorithm. The input declares each conflict once, so **build a symmetric adjacency list first**. And the graph may be in several pieces, so **loop over every uncoloured node**, not just the first.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Try every assignment. Each animal goes left or right, so enumerate all 2ⁿ combinations and check each against the conflict list. *O(2ⁿ · E) time, O(n) space.*

**Why not good enough.** Twenty animals is a million assignments and forty is a trillion. But the better objection is that it tells you nothing: it answers "is there one" without ever explaining why not, so no follow-up about three groups or about which pair caused the failure can be answered from it. Backtracking with propagation is the same algorithm as the colouring, arrived at without noticing.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `Dictionary<int, List<int>>` — animal to the animals it conflicts with |
| TRANSFORMATION | Build a **symmetric** adjacency list, adding both directions and creating an entry for any animal seen only as a value |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `Dictionary<int, int>` for the side of each animal, a `Queue<int>` for the BFS frontier |
| ALGORITHM | For every uncoloured animal, BFS assigning `1 - side[current]`; fail on an edge joining two animals already on the same side |
| OUTPUT | `true` if every component coloured cleanly, otherwise `false` |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Walk the input. For each key and each animal in its list, add the edge in **both** directions, creating either endpoint if it is new.
- Reject immediately if any animal conflicts with itself.
- For each animal in the adjacency list with no side yet: assign side 0 and push it.
- Pop a node. For each neighbour: if uncoloured, give it the opposite side and push it.
- If the neighbour already has a side and it **equals** the current node’s side, return false — an odd cycle.
- If every component finishes, return true.

- Two groups exactly. Not "at most two", and not three — three changes the problem completely, as the follow-up covers.
- An animal may appear only as a **value**, never as a key. It still has to be placed, so it still has to be in the graph.
- The conflict graph may have several disconnected components. Each is coloured independently, and a single BFS from one start node would miss the rest.
- The relation is symmetric even though the input may declare it once.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| A separate adjacency dictionary | Colouring the input map directly loses the animals that appear only as values, and forces you to check both directions on every edge. Building it once is cheaper and removes a whole class of bug. |
| `Dictionary<int, int>` for sides | Serves as both the visited set and the colour. Two structures would have to be kept consistent; one cannot drift. |
| `Queue` (BFS) rather than recursion | Either works. BFS avoids a stack overflow on a long chain, and the "colour is the opposite of the node I came from" rule reads more obviously in the iterative form. DFS with an explicit stack is equally fine — the recursion depth is the only real argument. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**Why `Touch` exists at all.** It creates an empty adjacency entry for an animal, and it is called for both endpoints of every edge. That one call is what handles the animal appearing only as a value — without it, animal 2 in `{1: [2]}` would never be a key in `adj`, and the outer loop would never consider it. A quietly missing node is the hardest bug to see here, because the answer is still a plausible boolean.

**The outer loop is the disconnected-components fix.** `foreach (int start in adj.Keys)` with `if (side.ContainsKey(start)) continue;`. A single BFS from one node explores one component. In my second example the invalid triangle is in the second component, so a single-start solution returns true — confidently wrong.

**Why `side` is both colour and visited set.** `side.TryGetValue` answers "have I seen this" and "which side" in one probe. Keeping a separate `HashSet<int> visited` alongside a colour map means two structures that must agree, and the bug when they disagree is a node coloured twice.

**The comparison that decides everything.** `colour == side[cur]` on an already-coloured neighbour. If it differs, the edge is satisfied and there is nothing to do — note that we do **not** re-enqueue. If it matches, the graph has an odd cycle. One comparison is the entire failure detection.

**Self-conflict, handled before the walk.** `if (other == pair.Key) return false;` during the build. A self-loop would otherwise be coloured as "neighbour already has my side" and produce the right answer by accident; handling it explicitly means the reason is in the code.

**Why `Split` re-walks instead of sharing state.** It is duplication, and deliberate: `CanSplit` is the answer to the question asked, and keeping it free of output-collection machinery keeps it readable. In production the two would be one function returning a result object. In an interview I would write `CanSplit` first, get agreement, and only then extend.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| build adjacency | O(V + E) | O(V + E) | Each declared conflict adds two directed entries |
| `CanSplit` | O(V + E) | O(V) | Every node enqueued once, every edge examined twice |
| `Split` | O(V + E) | O(V) | Same walk, plus the output lists |

V is the number of **distinct animals**, which is not the number of keys in the input map — animals appearing only as values count. That distinction is the complexity version of the same bug the `Touch` call prevents.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Empty or null map | Returns true. Nothing to place, so a valid split exists trivially. |
| An animal with an empty conflict list | Gets its own component of one node, coloured 0. Fine. |
| An animal only ever a value | Created by `Touch` and coloured normally. |
| Self-conflict `{1: [1]}` | Returns false during the build, before any colouring. |
| The same conflict declared twice | A parallel edge. The neighbour is already coloured and on the opposite side, so it is accepted and nothing is re-enqueued. |
| Several components, one invalid | Caught, because the outer loop reaches every component. This is the case a naive solution fails. |
| An even cycle | Valid. Only **odd** cycles are impossible, and stating that distinction is the difference between knowing the theorem and remembering a recipe. |
| A long chain of 100,000 animals | BFS is iterative, so no stack overflow. Recursive DFS would need a depth limit or an explicit stack. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Return the two groups, not just whether they exist.**

Partition the `side` dictionary by value. Animals with side 0 form one group, side 1 the other. Note that the assignment is not unique: any component can be flipped independently, so with k components there are 2ᵏ valid answers and any one of them is correct.

*Trade-off:* No extra cost. The only decision is what to do when no split exists — throw, or return the conflicting pair. Returning the pair is more useful, because a caller can then explain the failure to a user, and it costs only carrying the edge out of the walk.

**What if three groups were allowed?**

Two-colouring is decidable in linear time. **Three-colouring is NP-complete.** There is no known polynomial algorithm, so the honest answer changes shape: backtracking with constraint propagation for small inputs, a heuristic such as DSATUR (colour the most-constrained node first) for larger ones, and if this were real, a SAT or CP solver rather than hand-rolled search.

*Trade-off:* Exact and exponential, or approximate and fast. What matters in the interview is not the algorithm choice — it is recognising that a one-word change to the problem statement moved it across the tractability line, and saying so instead of confidently generalising the BFS.

**The conflict list arrives as a stream and never fits in memory. Now what?**

Union-find with parity is the right tool: keep, for each animal, its representative and whether it is the same side as that representative. Merging two animals that already share a representative **and** the same parity is the odd cycle, detected the instant the edge arrives. Almost constant time per edge, and it needs one pass with no adjacency list.

*Trade-off:* Union-find answers "is it still satisfiable" incrementally, which BFS cannot. It does not give you the groups as cheaply, and it cannot be undone — there is no efficient way to remove an edge. Trade the groups and deletion for O(1) streaming updates.

**Why BFS rather than DFS? Does it matter?**

Both visit every node once and both detect the same failure. BFS is iterative by construction, so a 100,000-node chain is fine; recursive DFS would overflow the stack. DFS has one genuine advantage: the recursion stack **is** the current path, so if you want to report the odd cycle itself, DFS hands it to you and BFS makes you reconstruct it from parent pointers.

*Trade-off:* BFS for robustness on deep graphs, DFS if the follow-up asks which cycle broke it. Choose on that basis rather than by habit.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Self-conflict? An animal with no conflicts? A one-way declaration?* — Self-conflict is unsplittable; isolated animals go anywhere; build the relation symmetric

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Complexity?* — O(V + E) time and space
